title: Backend breaking-change checks

story: Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, renames a field in the projects API from workgroup to workgroup_uid, because the ticket asked for clearer names. It is careful: it updates the serializer, every test and the frontend, and CI is green. A person approves, and the change ships on Tuesday.

On Wednesday a customer's nightly script fails. It uses the rhino-health SDK they installed from PyPI two months ago, and that SDK still sends workgroup, which the API now refuses. Nothing in the pull request was wrong by itself. The broken reader was simply not in the pull request, so no test, no compiler and no reviewer ever saw it.
hook.question: How can CI notice that a change breaks a reader who is not part of the pull request?

read.h: The readers you cannot see, and the merge base
p: In the frontend, tsc protects you from this kind of mistake: rename an exported field and every file that reads it turns red. That works because every reader is in the same repo. fcp's backend has readers outside the repo. The SDK on PyPI is installed by customers who upgrade months later. The on-prem client, installed in a customer's network, talks to the cloud over gRPC and is upgraded after the cloud. And during every deploy, yesterday's code keeps running for a few minutes on old servers while the database migration has already run. A change that one of these readers cannot handle is a breaking change, and no test inside the pull request can see it.

So every breaking-change check has the same shape: produce the contract as it was before the pull request, produce it as it is now, and compare. "Before" means the merge base, the last commit that the pull request's branch and main have in common, which git merge-base HEAD main prints. Comparing with the merge base instead of the newest main means the check sees only this pull request's changes, not other people's. To run the old code, you check out the merge base into a second folder with git worktree, which gives you two working copies of one repository side by side. CI jobs need fetch-depth: 0 for this, because a normal CI checkout downloads only the newest commit and has no merge base to find.

code.file: compare the API contract of a branch with its merge base
code.text:
base=$(git merge-base HEAD main)
git worktree add ../p10-5-base "$base"

(cd ../p10-5-base && uv run python manage.py spectacular --file ../p10-5/base.yaml)
uv run python manage.py spectacular --file head.yaml

docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" tufin/oasdiff \
  breaking /work/base.yaml /work/head.yaml --fail-on ERR

notes.text: The last commit this branch shares with main.
A second working copy of the repo at that commit, in a folder next to this one.
The old code writes the old contract. drf-spectacular reads the serializers and viewsets to produce it.
This branch writes the new contract.
Fail (exit 1) if any change is at error level.

p: OpenAPI is a standard YAML or JSON document that lists every endpoint of an HTTP API: its URL, parameters, request body and responses with their fields and types. fcp does not write it by hand. drf-spectacular generates it from the same serializers and viewsets that serve the requests, so it always describes the real code. oasdiff is a tool that reads two OpenAPI files and lists the differences that would break a client: a removed endpoint, a removed response field, a new required field in a request, a changed type.

Each finding has a level, error or warning, and --fail-on ERR makes the command exit with 1 when there is at least one error, which fails the CI job. For the rename from the story, oasdiff finds twenty changes, eleven of them errors, and the first two already show the whole problem. The fix is not to silence the check but to change the API in two steps. First add workgroup_uid next to workgroup, which no client notices; later, once every reader uses the new name, remove the old one in a separate, announced change. When a break is truly deliberate, a person records it with the ticket key in an ignore file that only people may change, because an agent must never change the checks it is judged by.
read.see:
$ docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" tufin/oasdiff breaking /work/base.yaml /work/head.yaml --fail-on ERR --format singleline
20 changes: 11 error, 9 warning, 0 info
error at /work/head.yaml, in API GET /api/projects/ removed the required property `items/workgroup` from the response with the `200` status [response-required-property-removed].
error at /work/head.yaml, in API POST /api/projects/ added the new required request property `workgroup_uid` (media type: application/json) [new-required-request-property].
…
$ echo $?
1

read.h: The same check for gRPC: buf breaking
p: The cloud and the on-prem client do not talk JSON. They use gRPC, a way to call a function on another machine, with the messages described in .proto files. Each field in a proto message has a number, and the number is what travels on the wire, not the name. So the rules are different from JSON: renaming a field changes the generated code that both sides compile against, and reusing or deleting a field number can make an old client read the wrong data.

buf is a tool for proto files, and buf breaking compares the protos in your branch with an older version, for example the main branch in git. With the PACKAGE rule set, which also protects the generated code, deleting or renaming a field is breaking. The safe change has the same two-step shape as for the JSON API: keep the old field, mark it deprecated, and add the new one with a new number.

notes.text: The old field stays, with its number, so old clients keep working. deprecated warns people who use it.
The new name gets a new number. Never reuse a number that was ever used.

read.see:
$ docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/workspace" -w /workspace bufbuild/buf:1.55.1 breaking proto --against '.git#branch=main,subdir=proto'
proto/projects/v1/projects.proto:8:3:Field "3" with name "workgroup_uid" on message "Project" changed option "json_name" from "workgroup" to "workgroupUid".
proto/projects/v1/projects.proto:8:10:Field "3" on message "Project" changed name from "workgroup" to "workgroup_uid".
$ echo $?
100

deeper.h: Go deeper: why PACKAGE and not WIRE
p: buf offers several rule sets. WIRE only asks whether bytes written by the old code can still be read by the new code, so it allows renaming fields and even deleting a whole method. PACKAGE also protects the generated code and the names, which is stricter.

fcp needs the stricter set because of how its cloud reaches the clients: one proxy service carries every call, and the request names the method to run as a string. A renamed method therefore still parses perfectly on the wire, and it still breaks every client that was installed before the rename.

read.h: Migrations break the code that is still running
p: A database migration has its own invisible reader: the old version of the application. During a deploy, the migration runs first, and for a few minutes the old servers keep serving requests with the old code. If the migration drops a column that the old code still selects, every one of those requests fails. django-migration-linter reads Django's migrations and reports operations like that. A second tool, Squawk, reads the SQL a migration will run (manage.py sqlmigrate prints it) and warns about locks: for example, adding a NOT NULL column takes a lock that blocks every read and write on the table while it runs, and on a big table that is an outage.

The safe pattern is called expand and contract. First expand: add the new column or field, and let the code write both. Then switch every reader to the new one. Only when nothing reads the old one, contract: remove it in a later deploy. The rename from the story would follow the same steps in the database as in the API.
read.see:
$ uv run python manage.py lintmigrations projects 0003_remove_project_archived
(projects, 0003_remove_project_archived)... ERR
	DROPPING columns (table: projects_project, column: archived)
*** Summary ***
Valid migrations: 0/1
Erroneous migrations: 1/1
$ uvx --from squawk-cli squawk add_not_null.sql
warning[require-lock-timeout]: Missing `set lock_timeout` before potentially slow ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock operations
warning[adding-required-field]: Adding a new column that is `NOT NULL` and has no default value to an existing table effectively makes it required.

deeper.h: Go deeper: two more checks, the published SDK and mutants
p: oasdiff compares documents, but a customer runs code. A smoke test closes that gap: it installs the latest released SDK from PyPI, starts the API of this commit as a real HTTP server inside the test (pytest-django's live_server fixture), and makes a few real calls such as logging in and creating a project. If the published SDK cannot talk to the new API, the test fails before any customer notices.

A different question is whether the tests themselves would notice a bug. Mutation testing answers it: a tool such as mutmut changes the code on purpose, for example turning > into >= or deleting a line, and runs the tests. Each changed version is a mutant. If the tests still pass, the mutant survived, which shows a piece of code that no test really checks. It is slow, so it runs at night on a few changed files and produces a report for people, never a required check.

lab.title: Catch the rename before it ships
lab.goal: Make the rename from the story on a branch, let oasdiff and buf compare it with the merge base, and change it so both checks pass.

guess.q: The branch renames workgroup to workgroup_uid in the serializer and updates every test. pytest is green. What does oasdiff breaking say when it compares the merge base's OpenAPI file with the branch's?

options.text: Nothing, because the tests prove the API still works.
options.why: The tests were updated together with the code, so they describe the new contract. oasdiff compares the contract with the old one, which is what outside readers still use.

options.text: Only a warning, because a rename is not a real removal.
options.why: For a client, a rename is a removal plus a new required field. oasdiff reports both as errors.

options.text: Errors: workgroup was removed from responses, and workgroup_uid is a new required request field.
options.why: Old clients read workgroup from the response and send workgroup in the request, so both directions break. --fail-on ERR exits with 1.

follow.say: Start from the projects API of p10-3, in a new folder, and add drf-spectacular, the library fcp uses to generate its OpenAPI file.
Register drf-spectacular in the settings and make it the schema generator.
Add a small proto file next to the API, the shape the cloud and the on-prem client use, with a buf.yaml that picks the PACKAGE rules.
Make this state the main branch, so there is a merge base to compare with.

lab.build: Make the rename safe in both contracts, the expand step of expand and contract. In the serializer, keep workgroup in the fields list and add workgroup_uid next to it as a read-only alias (serializers.CharField(source="workgroup", read_only=True)); your tests now send workgroup again. In the proto, put workgroup back as field 3 with [deprecated = true] and add workgroup_uid as field 4. Regenerate head.yaml and run both checks again.
checks: With the plain rename, oasdiff printed 11 errors and exit 1.
With the plain rename in the proto, buf printed changed name from "workgroup" to "workgroup_uid" and exit 100.
After your change, uv run pytest -q passes.
oasdiff now says No breaking changes to report, but the specs are different, and exit 0.
buf breaking prints nothing and exits 0.

solution.file: the safe rename in the serializer and the proto

lab.fix: A teammate made the red oasdiff job green: in their CI step, base.yaml is now generated with uv run python manage.py spectacular --file base.yaml in the branch's own folder, "because the worktree was slow". Do the same with the plain rename (git stash your fix first, or use a new branch) and run oasdiff: it says No changes detected. Explain what the check is comparing now, and put the merge-base step back.
explain: Why can no test inside the pull request catch the rename, even though the tests cover the endpoint?
Why does the check compare with the merge base and not with the newest commit on main?
In the proto, why is a new field number the safe way to rename, and what would reusing number 3 for a different meaning do to an old client?
lab.done: Both checks fail on the plain rename and pass on your expand step, and you removed the second working copy with git worktree remove ../p10-5-base.

check.q: A pull request removes a field from a response serializer and updates the tests and the frontend in the same pull request. Which reader can still break?

options.text: None; the tests and the frontend were updated.
options.why: They were updated because they live in the repo. Readers outside it were not.

options.text: An SDK version that customers installed from PyPI before this change.
options.why: Published packages keep the old contract until each customer upgrades, which can take months. That is why the API is compared with its old version.

options.text: The database, because the column still exists.
options.why: An unused column does not break anything. The danger is the reader that still expects the field.

check.q: The breaking-change job compares the branch's OpenAPI file with one generated from the newest commit on main instead of the merge base. What goes wrong?

options.text: The job also reports other people's changes that reached main after the branch started, so it blames the wrong pull request.
options.why: The merge base is the point where this branch left main. Comparing with it shows only this branch's changes.

options.text: Nothing; the newest main is always the better reference.
options.why: Main moves while the branch is open. The difference between main's tip and the branch mixes two sets of changes.

options.text: oasdiff refuses to compare files from different commits.
options.why: oasdiff compares any two files. Choosing the right two is your job.

check.q: You must rename a column that old servers still read during the deploy. Which order follows expand and contract?

options.text: Rename the column in one migration, because Django can do it in one step.
options.why: The old servers still read the old name for a few minutes after the migration runs, so every request they handle fails.

options.text: Remove the old column first, then add the new one in the same deploy.
options.why: That breaks the old code even more: it drops data that the running servers still read.

options.text: Add the new column and write both, move every reader to the new one, and drop the old column in a later deploy.
options.why: At every moment, the code that is running finds the column it expects.

p: fcp's cloud CI gets one check per invisible reader. oasdiff compares the OpenAPI file that drf-spectacular generates for the merge base and for the branch. django-migration-linter and Squawk check every new migration, first as advice and later as a blocking check. buf breaking compares the gRPC protos in common/fcp_common/rhinoAgentRpc with the merge base, using PACKAGE rules because the proxy carries method names as strings. A smoke test runs the published SDK against the branch's API, and a nightly, advisory mutation report shows which lines of yesterday's agent pull requests no test really checks.
A deliberate break is recorded by a person, with the ticket key, in an ignore file under a protected path, so that no agent can turn off the checks its work is judged by.

tickets.why: oasdiff on the merge base's and the branch's OpenAPI files, with a person-only ignore file.
django-migration-linter for the running old code and Squawk for locks, on every new migration.
buf breaking with PACKAGE rules on the cloud-client protos.
A smoke test that runs the published rhino-health SDK against this commit's API.
A nightly mutation report on files that agent pull requests changed.

words.plain: A change that a reader outside the pull request (an old SDK, an old client, old servers) cannot handle.
The last commit a branch and main have in common; git merge-base HEAD main prints it.
A standard document listing every endpoint of an HTTP API with its fields; fcp generates it with drf-spectacular.
A tool that compares two OpenAPI files and reports the changes that would break a client.
The command that compares proto files with an older version and reports breaking changes.
Change a contract in two deploys: add the new thing next to the old, then remove the old once nothing reads it.

review.q: Name three readers of fcp's backend that are not in the repo, and the check that protects each one.
review.a: The published SDK (oasdiff, plus the SDK smoke test), the on-prem client (buf breaking on the protos), and the old servers during a deploy (django-migration-linter and Squawk).

review.q: Write the two commands that produce base.yaml from the merge base in a second working copy.
review.a: git worktree add ../base "$(git merge-base HEAD main)", then run the schema export inside ../base and write its output to base.yaml.

review.q: How do you rename a JSON field and a proto field without breaking anyone?
review.a: Expand: add the new name next to the old one (a read-only alias in the serializer, a new field number in the proto, with the old one deprecated). Contract later, once every reader has moved.

remember: Readers outside the pull request only see the old contract, so CI compares the contract at the merge base with the branch's, and changes go in two steps: expand, then contract.
